paper_title: RoboColosseum: Evaluating Physical Intelligence at Scale In-The-Wild

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: General-purpose robot policies must work across robots, tasks, and environments, yet the variation that makes physical trials informative also makes them difficult to reproduce. We introduce RoboColosseum, a distributed evaluation framework that combines unified policy serving and standardized protocols across a network of locally operated robots in diverse environments. Our initial study evaluates five vision-language-action (VLA) policies and three frontier AI agents across four embodiments (SO-101, Franka, Bimanual-YAM, and G1 Humanoid). The Open Track compares models without task-specific adaptation in blinded, pairwise trials under matched local conditions. The Fine-tune Track measures how well VLA policies adapt to 20 tasks across all four embodiments when each policy receives the same 100 demonstrations per task. Across 5,699 pairwise Open Track comparisons at 124 sites, frontier agents rival specialized VLA policies, while all systems struggle to complete open-world tasks reliably. After fine-tuning, GR00T N1.7 leads on SO-101 and pi0.5 leads on Franka and Bimanual-YAM. Policy rankings show weak agreement across embodiment-specific task suites (Kendall W = 0.24). Open Track rankings poorly predict relative performance after fine-tuning, with substantial rank reversals on all three embodiments shared between tracks. Measuring partial progress reveals differences that task success alone misses. On the G1 Humanoid, no policy completes any of the five tasks, yet average progress ranges from 13.3% to 23.2% across policies. Open Track rankings stabilize as trials accumulate, and active matchmaking achieves comparable ranking agreement with substantially fewer physical trials than uniform sampling. These results show how distributed physical evaluation can reveal where robot policies generalize, how well they adapt to new tasks, and how far they progress on tasks they fail to complete.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: You dont know what you dont know. Socrates, Philosopher Recent advances in robot learning are shifting the field from policies tailored to individual tasks and platforms toward general-purpose models (Fang et al., 2026; Team et al., 2025; Intelligence et al., 2025; NVIDIA et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2025) trained across diverse tasks, environments, and embodiments (ONeill et al., 2024; 1 Figure 1 RoboColosseum overview. RoboColosseum connects distributed evaluation sites through shared robot interfaces, policy-serving infrastructure, and two complementary evaluation tracks. In the Fine-tune Track, policies receive the same 100 demonstrations per task and are evaluated on predefined tasks using common success and progress criteria. In the Open Track, policies are evaluated without additional task-specific adaptation through blinded, pairwise comparisons under matched local conditions, while tasks and environments vary across comparisons. The results shown for both tracks are based on evaluations we conducted from 17 September to 28 October 2026. The project spans SO-101, Franka in the DROID configuration, Bimanual-YAM, and Unitree G1, with participation determined by track and model compatibility. The lower panels illustrate track-specific evaluation outputs and examples of physical evaluation settings. The global network depicts the broader project vision; the scope of completed experiments is reported separately. Khazatsky et al., 2024). Although compelling demonstrations from leading robotics companies highlight the potential of these models (Dyna Robotics, 2026; Sunday Robotics, 2025; Skild AI Team, 2025; Generalist AI, 2026), establishing their reliability under real-world deployment conditions remains fundamental challenge. In language and vision, large-scale benchmarks incorporating human preferences on real-world tasks have helped drive progress by providing shared basis for assessing model capabilities relevant to end users (Zheng et al., 2023; Chiang et al., 2024a; Huang et al., 2024). Robot policies, by contrast, operate through closed-loop interactions with the physical world, where each action shapes the conditions for what follows. Evaluating them reliably is therefore difficult, especially at scale and in the varied, uncontrolled settings of the real world. Measuring progress requires understanding what robots can consistently accomplish across these conditions. Such assessments are difficult to standardize because outcomes depend jointly on the policy, robot setup, initial conditions, and surrounding environment (Vincent et al., 2024). Even nominally identical tasks can differ in object placement, camera configuration, lighting, and physical properties, making it difficult to attribute performance differences to policy capability. Physical evaluation must therefore reconcile two requirements: sufficient control to support meaningful comparisons and sufficient environmental diversity to assess robustness beyond particular setup. Simulation supports scalable evaluation through repeatable resets and controlled variation in tasks and environments (James et al., 2020; Tao et al., 2025). However, differences in sensing, calibration, dynamics, and visual appearance can limit how well simulated performance 2 predicts real-world outcomes, making physical validation essential (Li et al., 2024; Pumacay et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2026). Achieving comparable scale with physical robots requires substantial labor for setup, resets, hardware maintenance, and trial execution. Consequently, real-world studies often rely on relatively few rollouts, leaving performance estimates sensitive to trial selection and experimental variability (Kress-Gazit et al., 2024; Vincent et al., 2024). Distributing evaluation across sites broadens environmental coverage (Khazatsky et al., 2024; Atreya et al., 2025), but efforts that depend on students and volunteers are difficult to sustain and scale. Running physical trials requires continued staffing, equipment maintenance, and coordination across sites, often alongside competing research commitments. Sustained evaluation therefore requires dedicated operators and shared physical infrastructure, supported by protocols for repeating trials, matching local conditions, and verifying whether measured performance can be reproduced. We introduce RoboColosseum, distributed, multi-embodiment benchmark for evaluating general-purpose robot policies in the wild. It connects geographically distributed sites through unified evaluation and policyserving infrastructure, with standardized hardware configurations, task definitions, and evaluation protocols. The benchmark initially supports four embodiments Bimanual-YAM, SO-101, Franka, and Unitree G1 and evaluates eight foundation models: five vision-language-action (VLA) policies and three frontier LLMs. Two complementary tracks assess adaptation and generalization. The Fine-tune Track measures performance on predefined semantic tasks after adaptation using fixed budget of task-specific demonstrations. The Open Track evaluates zero-shot generalization across diverse real-world tasks and environments without taskspecific adaptation. Together, they enable systematic assessment of physical intelligence across heterogeneous embodiments. With growing fleet of over 100 robots across the United States, United Kingdom, Singapore, Malaysia, and China, operated by full-time evaluators, RoboColosseum aims to make real-world evaluation scalable and sustainable. This shared infrastructure provides lens into the capabilities and limitations of robot foundation models, enabling the research community to investigate fundamental scientific questions through systematic physical trials. To broaden access, we pledge 10,000 hours of free evaluation to academic labs and partners. Our initial study includes 5,699 Open Track pairwise comparisons across 124 sites and Fine-tune Track evaluations on 20 tasks across four embodiments. Frontier AI agents achieve manipulation performance competitive with specialized VLA policies, while reliable task completion remains challenging as task difficulty increases. With the same 100-demonstration adaptation budget, policies exhibit strongly taskand embodimentdependent performance, with weak agreement in rankings across embodiments (W = 0.24) and substantial rank reversals between the Open and Fine-tune Tracks. Finally, leaderboard stability improves with evaluation scale, while active matchmaking reaches approximately 90% agreement with the full-data ranking after 400500 evaluations, compared with roughly 1,000 under uniform sampling. These findings demonstrate the importance of evaluating physical intelligence across diverse tasks, embodiments, and environments, while showing that large-scale real-world evaluation can be made statistically reliable and sample-efficient.

sections.title:
2.1 Simulated and Real-World Benchmarking
Real-world robot benchmarks aim to make physical policy evaluation more reproducible despite variation in
hardware, calibration, object placement, and scene reset. These factors can substantially affect measured
performance, motivating standardized hardware, task definitions, initial conditions, and success criteria (Kress-
Gazit et al., 2024). Early benchmarks such as FurnitureBench improve comparability by prescribing a common
robot platform, workspace, objects, and task protocols (Heo et al., 2025), while SceneReplica further studies
reproducibility by reconstructing physical scenes using reference images and calibrated setups (Khargonkar
et al., 2024). Remote testbeds such as TOTO and the Real Robot Challenge instead centralize physical
hardware and allow researchers to submit policies for evaluation on a shared robot platform, reducing variation
caused by independently constructed setups (Zhou et al., 2023; Bauer et al., 2022).
sections.content: More recent benchmarks extend these ideas toward broader policy and embodiment coverage (Pumacay et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026). RoboDojo (Chen et al., 2026) evaluates 18 3 real-world tasks across three bimanual robot platforms using standardized workspaces, reset procedures, and sub-step scoring, while VLA-REPLICA provides low-cost SO-101 setup designed to be reconstructed at different locations (Chen et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026). RoboColosseum builds on this line of work while targeting broader physical coverage across multiple embodiments and sites under shared evaluation protocols.

sections.title:
2.2 Generalist Robot Policies
Generalist robot policies seek to transfer learned skills across tasks, environments, and embodiments. RT-X
models demonstrate that pooling demonstrations from different robots can improve performance through
transfer across platforms (O’Neill et al., 2024). Octo provides a pretrained policy that can be adapted to
new observation and action spaces (Team et al., 2024). Vision-language-action models such as OpenVLA
combine pretrained vision-language representations with robot demonstrations to predict actions from
visual observations and language instructions, while supporting fine-tuning on demonstrations from a target
setting (Kim et al., 2024).
sections.content: Recent models extend these capabilities through diverse training data and different approaches to action generation. π0.5 combines data from multiple robots with web data and semantic supervision to support manipulation in previously unseen homes (Black et al., 2025). GR00T combines vision-language processing with dedicated action-generation module (Bjorck et al., 2025), while MolmoAct2 connects backbone trained for embodied reasoning to continuous-action expert (Fang et al., 2026). These models provide different approaches to combining semantic knowledge with physical control. General-purpose language models can also guide robot behavior through skill selection or program generation. SayCan selects learned robot skills using both language-model predictions and estimates of execution success (Ahn et al., 2022), while Code as Policies generates programs that process perception outputs and call robot control APIs (Liang et al., 2022). RoboColosseum compares VLA policies and frontier AI agents across physical environments and embodiments without task-specific adaptation, and separately measures how VLA policies adapt using common budget of task demonstrations.

sections.title:
2.3 Distributed Robotics Evaluation
Distributed evaluation provides an alternative to tightly centralized robot benchmarks by allowing policies to
be tested across heterogeneous physical environments while aggregating results into a common comparison.
RB2 is an early example, distributing manipulation evaluation across multiple laboratories while controlling
task definitions and aggregating site-specific rankings rather than directly comparing raw scores across different
physical setups (Dasari et al., 2021). More recently, RoboArena extends this idea to generalist robot policies
through a decentralized evaluation network spanning seven academic institutions. Evaluators freely select
tasks and environments, while each local comparison evaluates two anonymously assigned policies back-to-back
under matched scene conditions. Across 612 pairwise comparisons, RoboArena showed that rankings derived
from distributed evaluations correlate more strongly with an exhaustive oracle ranking than conventional fixed
single-site evaluation (Atreya et al., 2025). However, RoboArena is instantiated on a single DROID/Franka
embodiment, and its open-ended decentralized design makes controlled single-factor experiments difficult.
sections.content: Pairwise comparison has also been widely used for arena-style evaluation. Chatbot Arena ranks anonymized models from human pairwise preferences using BradleyTerry-based estimation (Chiang et al., 2024b), while active-ranking methods show that comparisons can be allocated toward more informative model pairs rather than sampled uniformly (Heckel et al., 2018). These ideas provide methodological precedent for RoboColosseums Open Track, where pairwise physical evaluations are aggregated into global ranking and costly robot trials can be prioritized toward uncertain model pairs.

sections.title:
3.1 Physical Infrastructure and Operational Protocols
RoboColosseum currently supports four robot embodiments spanning diverse costs, morphologies, and control
complexities: a low-cost single arm, a bimanual system, a research-grade arm, and a walking humanoid
(Table 1). Evaluating the same model families across these embodiments tests whether findings generalize
across hardware platforms, a question single-embodiment benchmarks cannot address. To sustain reliable
daily evaluation at scale, we establish standardized hardware configurations, setup procedures, and operational
protocols across sites.
sections.content: Embodiments and Compute. RoboColosseum supports SO-101, Bimanual YAM, Franka, and the G1 humanoid, with standardized hardware configurations adapted for deployment in unstructured environments. SO-101 uses single external camera following common community configurations, while Bimanual YAM adopts the MolmoAct2 setup; both systems are mounted on mobile trolleys. The Franka platform follows the DROID (Khazatsky et al., 2024) configuration, and G1 is equipped with parallel grippers, all of which are shown in Figure 2 Policy inference runs either locally on laptop equipped with an RTX 5090 GPU or remotely through server-hosted endpoint in which both are operating by remote routing server. We measure inference and communication latency to verify that both configurations support low-latency execution. Sites and Operation Academic robot evaluation typically relies on controlled laboratory tasks and environments. RoboColosseum conducts all evaluations at real-world sites, including offices, libraries, parks, 5 dormitories, homes, food courts, and factories. Our evaluation network spans campuses and industry buildings in Singapore, homes in Malaysia, and factories in China, supporting the evaluation of diverse embodiments and deployment conditions. To sustain this effort, we hire up to 30 full-time robot operators execute evaluation protocols, reset task environments, and assess policy rollouts, with staffing expanding alongside evaluation demand. dedicated data-processing pipeline applies face blurring and identity anonymization to evaluation recordings to protect participant privacy.

sections.title:
3.2 Benchmark Design
RoboColosseum is designed to support evaluation in different real-world settings while keeping model compar-
isons fair. We do not require every site to use the same environment, objects, or background. Instead, the
benchmark uses two evaluation tracks with different controls. In the Fine-tune Track, models are evaluated
on predefined tasks using a common adaptation and evaluation protocol. In the Open Track, models are
tested on diverse tasks and environments, but the two models in each comparison are evaluated under the
same local conditions.
sections.content: For each track, we clearly define what is fixed and what can vary. In the Fine-tune Track, models receive the same task-specific demonstration data and are evaluated using the same task definition, success criteria, progress criteria, and evaluation procedure. The training method can differ across models because different policy architectures require different fine-tuning procedures. This follows the controlled benchmark design used in DataComp, where selected factors are fixed so that different submissions can be compared under the same evaluation setting (Gadre et al., 2023). In the Open Track, models cannot use task-specific adaptation, while the task and environment can vary across evaluations. Within each pairwise comparison, the robot, task instruction, objects, initial setup, and timeout are kept the same.

sections.title:
3.2.1 Fine-tune Track
The Fine-tune Track evaluates how efficiently pretrained policies adapt to new tasks through rapid fine-
tuning on task-specific demonstrations. By holding the adaptation data and evaluation protocol fixed, this
track compares models’ ability to learn from the same demonstrations under consistent conditions, enabling
reproducible evaluation and fair comparison.
sections.content: Tasks. For each embodiment, RoboColosseum maintains an extensible registry of manipulation tasks, of which five per embodiment, 20 in total, are included in the current evaluation (Section B). Each task is specified by task card that defines the natural-language instruction, the objects, the initial setup, the success criteria, the timeout, the evaluation site, and set of task-specific progress criteria. The tasks span pick-and-place, stacking (bowls, cubes, and cups), object reorientation (standing fallen bottle upright), articulated objects (drawers, laptop lid, and microwave door), deformable objects (towels and clothing), liquid pouring, tool use (sweeping with dustpan and brush), bimanual coordination tasks with the bimanual YAMs, and loco-manipulation with the G1 Humanoid. Data Collection. For each task, we collect 100 high-quality teleoperated demonstrations using embodimentspecific interfaces: GELLO (Wu et al., 2024) for Bimanual-YAM, leaderfollower arm setup for SO-101 joint-space control, the DROID Quest teleoperation system for Franka DROID, and Pico VR headset with an off-the-shelf whole-body controller for the G1 humanoid. Demonstrations are collected at the evaluation site using the same robot and environment to match deployment conditions. All policies are fine-tuned on the same demonstrations, which we publicly release. Fine-tuning protocol. Each evaluated model is fully fine-tuned from its base pretrained checkpoint using the same 100 demonstrations, which constitute the only embodimentand task-specific data used during adaptation. Each policy follows its official fine-tuning recipe until convergence, allowing optimization schedules and training durations to vary across architectures. We thus control the adaptation data and evaluation protocol while allowing model-specific training procedures. The full protocol, base checkpoints, and per-model hyperparameters are provided in Section A. This design complements DataComp (Gadre et al., 2023): we hold the data fixed and vary the training procedure, rather than the reverse. 6 Evaluation and metrics. After fine-tuning, each policy is evaluated for = 25 trials per task using its original inference implementation. The task goal remains fixed, while object placements and environmental conditions may vary within the task specification. Each task is evaluated using task-specific progress criteria. sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: We conducted in-the-wild evaluations with RoboColosseum over duration of 41 days, from 17 September 2026 to 28 October 2026. We evaluated eight models across the Fine-Tune and Open Tracks: five visionlanguage-action (VLA) models and three frontier models. Using these results, we investigate the following research questions: RQ1: Open-world capabilities. What capabilities and failure modes do general-purpose robot models exhibit across diverse real-world tasks and environments? RQ2: Task adaptation. How effectively do pretrained robot policies adapt to unseen manipulation tasks given fixed budget of task-specific demonstrations? RQ3: Performance consistency. How consistent are model rankings across evaluation tracks and robot embodiments? RQ4: Evaluation reliability and efficiency. How reliably can distributed pairwise evaluations estimate model rankings, and how much can active matchmaking reduce the number of physical trials required? RQ5: Effect of evaluation scale. How does the number of physical evaluations affect ranking uncertainty and the stability of the Open Track leaderboard?

sections.title:
4.1 Experimental Setup
Models and protocols. We evaluate five VLA models—GR00T N1.7 (NVIDIA et al., 2025), π0.5 (Black et al.,
2025), MolmoAct2 (Fang et al., 2026), G0.5 (Liu et al., 2026), and LingBot-VLA v2 (Wu et al., 2026)—and
three API-accessible frontier models: GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, and Grok 4.7. The Fine-tune Track
evaluates VLA models initialized from base pretrained checkpoints on 20 tasks across four embodiments,

Points show posterior mean DCR ratings on an Elo-style scale, with 95% credible intervals; is the number of evaluations involving each system. with five tasks per embodiment, 100 demonstrations per task, and 25 evaluation trials per modeltask pair. The Open Track comprises 5,699 pairwise comparisons across 5,699 tasks, 124 sites, and four embodiments, following Section 3. VLA models use embodiment-specific checkpoints in this track; frontier-model agents participate exclusively in this track through the interface in Section 3.1. Metrics and statistical analysis. For the Fine-tune Track, we report success rate (SR) and normalized progress score (PS), and assess fine-tuning differences through paired comparisons with multiple-comparison correction. For the Open Track, DCR serves as the primary leaderboard metric, with BradleyTerryDavidson (BTD), sequential Elo, and average pairwise score as ranking baselines. For category-level analysis, we fit separate progress-based BTD model within each manipulation category: higher normalized task progress determines the winner, and equal progress yields tie. We report each systems expected comparison score, defined as its probability of winning plus half its probability of tying against hypothetical system of average ability; 50% thus indicates average relative performance within that category. We report uncertainty for success rates and model ratings, quantify ranking consistency using Spearmans correlation and pairwise ordering agreement, and assess ranking stability through repeated subsampling at increasing evaluation budgets.

sections.title: 4.2 Open-World Capabilities (RQ1)
sections.content: Frontier agents achieve competitive manipulation performance, but performance varies across agents and embodiments. Success-based DCR rankings show that frontier AI models can achieve competitive manipulation performance compared with specialized VLA policies, although their relative strengths differ across robot embodiments. In Figure 3, GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest DCR point estimate on DROID/Franka, whereas Claude Opus 5.5 leads on SO-101 and Bimanual-YAM. This competitiveness is also reflected in normalized task progress. Across 901 paired evaluations, agents achieve greater progress in 394 comparisons, VLAs in 265, and the remaining 242 are tied, yielding an average agent advantage of 5.3 percentage points (Figure 4). However, this advantage is not consistent across agents: Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra achieve mean advantages of 12.1 and 11.0 percentage points, respectively, whereas Grok 4.7 trails its VLA counterparts by 7.5 points. Together, these findings show that frontier agents can match or outperform specialized VLA policies in physical manipulation, but their relative performance depends on the agent and robot embodiment. Strong relative performance does not necessarily translate into reliable task completion. To examine manipulation capabilities beyond aggregate model rankings, we group Open Track tasks into six categories: Pick/Place, Stack/Arrange, Open/Close, Reorient, Deformable, and Tool/Interaction, using fixed languagemodel classifier following RoboArena (Atreya et al., 2025) (details in Appendix D.2). (a) Percentage of comparisons in which the agent makes more progress, the VLA makes more progress, or both make equal progress. Numbers inside the bars show comparison counts. (b) Mean difference in task progress (agent minus VLA, in percentage points), with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Positive values favor the agent. estimated BTD comparison scores for each manipulation category, while (b)(c) report mean normalized task progress and full-task success rates. MolmoAct2 achieves the highest BTD point estimate among the five VLA policies in all six categories, with expected comparison scores ranging from 58% to 77%. Despite this relative advantage, its observed task success rates range from only 6% to 13%, and no evaluated system exceeds 13% success in any category. Although absolute success rates also depend on the tasks and embodiments evaluated for each system, the consistently low success rates across all six categories suggest that current policies limitations extend beyond individual manipulation skills, with even the strongest evaluated systems struggling to reliably complete diverse open-world tasks. Policies struggle to make meaningful progress on the most difficult manipulation tasks. We examine how physical execution performance varies across human-rated task difficulty levels (Figure 6). Full-task success decreases sharply with difficulty, from 30.7% on tasks rated 14 to just 0.4% on tasks rated 910. This decline extends beyond task completion: mean normalized progress also falls from 56.6% to 3.5% across the same difficulty ranges, indicating that policies satisfy substantially fewer intermediate progress criteria on more challenging tasks. Although these trends are observational and may partly reflect differences in task and embodiment composition, they reveal that current policies struggle not only to complete difficult tasks, but also to make meaningful progress toward their goals. On the most challenging tasks, failures appear to arise well before the final success condition, suggesting that current policies lack the capabilities needed to execute even substantial portions of complex manipulation tasks. Takeaway. Frontier AI agents achieve manipulation performance competitive with specialized VLA policies, although their relative strengths vary across agents and robot embodiments. However, reliable open-world manipulation remains challenge for both types of systems: even the strongest policies achieve low task completion rates across manipulation categories, and their ability to make meaningful progress declines sharply on more difficult tasks. These findings highlight fundamental limitation of current robot policies: while they demonstrate promising manipulation capabilities, they struggle to sustain successful execution as task complexity increases.

4.4 Performance Consistency (RQ3)
Strong open-world performance does not consistently predict post-fine-tuning performance. Figure 9
compares the relative rankings of five VLA policies between the Open Track and Fine-tune Track. The
rankings show limited agreement across all three shared embodiments, with Spearman’s ρ = −0.20 on
SO-101, −0.40 on DROID/Franka, and 0.20 on Bimanual-YAM. Only 4, 3, and 6 of the 10 model pairs,
respectively, preserve their relative ordering between tracks. For example, π0.5 ranks fifth among VLA
policies on DROID/Franka in the Open Track but first after fine-tuning, and similarly moves from fourth
to first on Bimanual-YAM. Conversely, G0.5 ranks second on DROID/Franka in the Open Track but fifth
after fine-tuning. These comparisons involve only five policies, and the tracks differ in task distributions,
starting checkpoints, and ranking metrics, so the disagreement cannot be attributed solely to differences in
generalization and adaptation capabilities. Nevertheless, the observed rank reversals show that a policy’s
relative strength in open-world execution does not necessarily carry over to its performance after task-specific
adaptation.
sections.content: Relative policy strengths vary across robot embodiments and task settings. Figures 3 and 10a show that policy rankings vary across robot embodiments in both evaluation tracks. In the Open Track, the relative ordering of VLA policies changes across SO-101, DROID/Franka, and Bimanual-YAM, with different policies achieving the highest DCR ratings on each embodiment. Similar differences emerge in the Fine-tune Track, where Kendalls coefficient of concordance (W = 0.24) indicates limited agreement in policy rankings across the four embodiment-specific task suites. For example, π0.5 ranks first on both DROID/Franka and BimanualYAM but fourth on Unitree G1, whereas GR00T N1.7 leads on SO-101 but ranks fourth on DROID/Franka and Bimanual-YAM. Because each embodiment involves different tasks and environments, these differences cannot be attributed to robot morphology alone. Together, these findings show that relative policy strengths 13 Figure 8 Policy-specific failure stages after fine-tuning. We show two tasks whose progress criteria form an ordered sequence: SO-101 cube_drawer and DROID/Franka close_laptop. Each bar divides policys 25 evaluation trials into full-task successes (green) and failures, shaded by the first criterion the trial did not meet (darker red indicates an earlier failure). Numbers give trial counts; segments of single trial are unlabeled. Policies trained on the same demonstrations exhibit markedly different failure locations, revealing taskand policy-specific execution bottlenecks that are hidden by success rate alone. do not consistently carry across robot-task settings, whether evaluated without task-specific adaptation or after fine-tuning. Takeaway. Relative policy strengths vary across both evaluation tracks and robot-task settings. Policies that perform well without task-specific adaptation do not necessarily achieve similarly strong results after fine-tuning, and those that lead on one embodiment may perform less competitively on others. Together, these findings show that current general-purpose robot policies exhibit limited consistency in their relative performance across different evaluation conditions, with no single policy maintaining clear advantage across all settings.

sections.title: 4.5 Ranking Reliability and Efficiency (RQ4)
sections.content: Distributed pairwise evaluations produce broadly consistent rankings across independent site subsets. Figure 10b tests whether independent subsets of the distributed evaluation network produce the same DCR ranking. For each embodiment, we repeatedly partition the set of evaluation sites at random into two approximately equal, non-overlapping groups, assigning all evaluations from the same site to the same group, then fit DCR independently on each subset, and measure the fraction of model pairs whose relative ordering is preserved. DROID/Franka and Bimanual-YAM achieve mean pairwise ranking agreement of approximately 85%, with mean Spearman correlations of ρ = 0.82, indicating that substantially different subsets of sites recover similar model orderings. In contrast, SO-101 achieves only 59% agreement and ρ = 0.30, showing that its ranking is considerably more sensitive to which evaluation sites are included. These results indicate that distributed pairwise evaluation can produce reproducible rankings when sufficient evidence is available, but reliability is not uniform across embodiments. Active matchmaking recovers stable rankings with substantially fewer physical evaluations. Figure 11a compares uncertainty-driven active matchmaking with uniform sampling using the same DCR ranking estimator. Active matchmaking reaches approximately 90% agreement with the full-data ranking after only 400500 evaluations, whereas uniform sampling requires roughly 1,000 evaluations to achieve comparable agreement. The advantage is largest at limited evaluation budgets and diminishes as both strategies approach the full-data ranking, showing that active matchmaking improves sample efficiency without changing the underlying ranking objective. 14 Figure 9 Cross-track ranking consistency by embodiment. Open Track and Fine-tune Track rankings of the five VLA policies on (a) SO-101, (b) DROID/Franka, and (c) Bimanual-YAM. For each embodiment, the Open Track rank is computed from the DCR rating, while the Fine-tuning rank is computed from the mean progress score (PS) across its five tasks. Rank 1 denotes the best-performing model, and the dashed diagonal indicates identical rankings across the two tracks. Each panel reports Spearmans rank correlation and the number of model pairs with the same relative ordering in both tracks. Takeaway. Distributed pairwise evaluation can recover reproducible model rankings across independent subsets of evaluation sites, although reliability depends on the amount and distribution of evidence available for each embodiment. Active matchmaking further improves efficiency by directing physical trials toward the comparisons that are most informative for resolving the leaderboard.

sections.title: 4.6 Effect of scaling evaluation (RQ5)
sections.content: Leaderboard stability improves steadily with evaluation scale, but high-confidence stability requires substantially more data. Figure 11b measures how closely DCR rankings estimated from random subsets of the Open Track data match the ranking obtained from the full dataset. As the number of physical A/B comparisons increases, the mean agreement in model-pair ordering rises steadily, reaching 90% at approximately 1,123 evaluations and 95% at approximately 4,755 evaluations. However, the 2.5th97.5th percentile range remains substantially wider than the mean trend, showing that different subsets of the same size can still produce noticeably different rankings. Thus, relatively few evaluations are sufficient to recover most of the final ordering on average, while substantially more evaluations are required for the leaderboard to become consistently stable across different subsets of the data. Takeaway. More physical evaluations improve both ranking stability and confidence in the Open Track leaderboard. The average model ordering emerges relatively early, but establishing ranking that is robust to which evaluations are included requires much larger evaluation budget.

sections.title: 5 Limitations & Conclusion
sections.content: Conclusion. RoboColosseum provides distributed framework for measuring physical intelligence across real robots, tasks, environments, and evaluation settings. Our results show that no single evaluation captures model capability completely: frontier AI agents can be competitive with specialized VLA policies without task-specific adaptation, fine-tuned policies exhibit strongly taskand embodiment-dependent strengths, and relative model rankings can change across both evaluation tracks and robot platforms. Progress-based evaluation further reveals meaningful behavioral differences that binary task success alone can hide. 15 (a) Cross-embodiment ranking consistency (b) Consistency of DCR rankings across subsets Figure 10 Ranking consistency. a. Cross-embodiment ranking consistency based on Fine-tune Track progress score (PS) across SO-101, DROID, Bimanual-YAM, and Unitree G1. Rank 1 denotes the best-performing model on an embodiment. The substantial changes in model ordering across embodiments, together with Kendalls coefficient of concordance = 0.24, indicate weak agreement between embodiment-specific rankings. b. Consistency of DCR rankings across independent evaluation-site subsets. For each embodiment, evaluation sites are repeatedly divided into two disjoint subsets, and DCR is fit independently on each half. Points show the mean fraction of model pairs whose relative ordering agrees between the two rankings, and error bars show the 2.5th97.5th percentile across valid random splits. The annotated ρ is the mean Spearman rank correlation between the two rankings. Higher values indicate that the leaderboard is less sensitive to which subset of evaluation sites contributes the data. At the same time, large-scale pairwise evaluation makes these comparisons increasingly reproducible, while active matchmaking can concentrate costly physical trials on the comparisons that are most informative for resolving the leaderboard. Together, these results suggest that evaluating physical intelligence requires not only more capable models, but also sufficiently diverse, large-scale, and statistically grounded real-world evaluation. RoboColosseum provides the infrastructure and protocols for carrying out such evaluation as the model, task, embodiment, and site coverage continue to grow. Limitations. The current study represents an initial snapshot of RoboColosseum rather than an exhaustive evaluation of all robot foundation models and deployment settings. Coverage differs across model families and embodiments because participation depends on checkpoint and hardware compatibility, while the Fine-tune Track currently evaluates five tasks per embodiment. Future evaluations can naturally extend the benchmark with additional models, tasks, embodiments, and sites while retaining the same protocols. In the Fine-tune Track, we fix the task-specific demonstrations and evaluation procedure but allow each policy to use its official adaptation recipe. The resulting comparison therefore measures practical end-to-end adaptation from the same data rather than isolating architectural differences under an identical optimizer and training schedule. In the Open Track, our ranking-stability analyses quantify reproducibility relative to the leaderboard estimated from the complete collected dataset; as the benchmark grows, the same analyses can be repeated to measure how rankings evolve with broader evaluation coverage.

sections.title: 6 The Future
sections.content: RoboColosseum is long-term scientific megaproject designed to help the robotics community distinguish meaningful progress from noise through standardized evaluation protocols and large-scale, in-the-wild model deployment and testing. Its founding members; NUS MAGIC Lab, Hugging Face, the Singapore Embodied AI Centre, and BitRobot are committed to advancing this effort and enabling new scientific insights through real-world evaluation at scale. We pledge to expand the task datasets available for the fine-tuning track, provide access to more in-the-wild environments for open-track evaluation, and incorporate broader range of robotic embodiments. sections.content: A Fine-tune Track Training Protocol All Fine-tune Track models are trained with common harness designed for fair comparison under fixed data. Each VLA is trained with its own upstream repository, pinned to fixed commit and left unmodified. The harness adds only the components around it: conversion of the demonstrations into each models data format, per-model configurations registered from outside the repositories, and launch scripts. Settings shared by all models are listed in Table 3, and the per-model hyperparameters in Table 4. Table 3 Fine-tuning settings shared by all models. For GR00T N1.7, the full vision-language backbone is fine-tuned together with the action head, and the effective batch size is kept at 64. An earlier configuration that trained only the action head with an effective batch size of 512 received too few optimizer updates within five epochs and converged to constant prediction. SO-101 is an exception; we follow the default configuration, keeping the vision-language backbone frozen while training the projector and action-model components. For π0.5, the Aloha-specific action-space adaptation in the recipe is disabled, since none of the evaluated embodiments is an Aloha platform. Fine-tune Track Task Details We provide the full specification of the five fine-tuning tasks for each of the four embodiments (SO101, DROID, YAM, and G1). Each card shows the workspace and object setup photos together with the task instruction, objects used, object setup, success criteria, evaluation location, environment, timeout, and the partial progress criteria used for scoring. Fine-tune Track Per-Task Progress Reachability Figures 1215 decompose the embodiment-level reachability curves in Figure 7 into individual tasks. The results show that the aggregate differences between policies are driven by task-specific strengths and failures rather than by uniform advantage across every task. SO-101. Figure 12 shows that relatively simple tasks such as stack_bowls and upright_bottle preserve high progress for several policies, while more compositional tasks separate them more clearly. stack_cubes is particularly discriminative: several policies reach the initial interaction criteria, but their curves diverge sharply as the task requires completion of the multi-object stack. cube_drawer shows similar but less extreme pattern, indicating that grasping and transporting the cube is easier than completing the full placement-and-drawer sequence. These differences explain why the embodiment averages remain separated even when several models perform similarly on the easier SO-101 tasks. DROID. Figure 13 exhibits stronger task-specific specialization. close_laptop separates policies that can initiate contact from those that can reliably finish the articulated-object manipulation. open_drawer produces different ordering, with LingBot-VLA v2 maintaining high reachability while several other models lose progress rapidly after the initial interaction. marker_in_holder again changes the ordering, with MolmoAct2, GR00T N1.7, and π0.5 retaining substantially more progress than LingBot-VLA v2 and G0.5. towel_in_basket is comparatively favorable to several policies. The same robot embodiment therefore produces markedly different model rankings depending on the manipulation being evaluated. Bimanual-YAM. Figure 14 shows similar pattern under tasks requiring coordination between two arms. π0.5 maintains strong reachability across most tasks, while G0.5 is also competitive on several drawer, microwave, 29 Figure 13 Per-task progress reachability on DROID. Percentage of the 25 trials per model satisfying at least given fraction of the tasks progress criteria. and table-cleaning tasks. stack_cups produces substantially larger drops for multiple policies, indicating that completing the full multi-object arrangement is harder than satisfying its earlier criteria. The safety-stopped evaluations for LingBot-VLA v2 on drawer and GR00T N1.7 on microwave are shown separately and should be interpreted as truncated evaluations rather than ordinary performance curves. G1. Figure 15 produces the clearest gap between partial progress and complete success. None of the five policies completes any evaluated G1 task, yet their reachability curves show different amounts of partial execution. On tasks such as carry_box and load_clothes_washing_machine, some policies satisfy substantial fraction of the task criteria, but few trials satisfy the remaining requirements. plate_into_rack also shows measurable early progress, whereas fold_towel and hang_keys remain difficult for most policies. These results demonstrate why binary success alone is insufficient in the humanoid setting: although every policy has the same full-task outcome, the fraction of task criteria they satisfy clearly differs.

sections.content: D.1 Frontier AI Agents Three API-accessible agents, Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra, and Grok 4.7, are evaluated in the Open Track on SO-101, DROID, and Bimanual-YAM. Agents are used as released, with no fine-tuning, no taskspecific prompting, and no access to demonstrations. They are served through the Inspect Robots agent policy (Robocurve, 2026) running inside the RoboColosseum policy server, so task assignment, robot control, timeouts, and scoring are identical to those used for VLA policies. Table 5 lists the model identifiers and API settings, and Listing 1 gives the full system prompt. 30 Figure 14 Per-task progress reachability on Bimanual-YAM. Percentage of completed trials satisfying at least given fraction of the tasks progress criteria. Hollow markers denote evaluations stopped early for safety, with the number of completed trials given in the panel title; all other curves use 25 trials. Observation and action interface. At each decision step the agent receives the embodiments observation specification: the current images from all cameras of the embodiment at 640 480 (two views for SO-101 and DROID, three for Bimanual-YAM), the proprioceptive state as labeled numeric vector, and the language instruction. Images from the two most recent observations are kept in the conversation; older observations are kept as text only. fixed system prompt per embodiment describes the robot, its joint ordering and gripper convention, its workspace and camera placement, and the available tools. The agent acts through exactly one tool call per turn: move tool that specifies an absolute target, done, which declares the task complete, or give_up. On all three embodiments the target is joint-position vector in the embodiments action space, which the server interpolates into trajectory executed at fixed fraction of the rigs joint speed. Each move call must also include oneor two-sentence note describing what the agent observes and why it chose the motion; these notes are stored with the transcript. After each motion completes, the client returns the new observation and the loop continues until the agent calls done or give_up, or the trial reaches its step limit. The agents own done never counts as success. Execution and safety. Every returned trajectory is validated on the server against calibrated joint limits and per-step joint-change limits before execution, truncated to the embodiments maximum chunk length, and re-planned from the next measured state; the client applies the same joint clipping to agent and VLA actions alike. Agents are queried with reasoning effort set to medium and at most 30 model calls per trial; each trial is limited to 800 control steps, and call that exceeds the per-call inference deadline of 120 is discarded and the trial continues from the next observation. Because every decision requires round trip to the providers API, agents act at much lower rate than VLA policies, while the trial step limit is the same for all models within comparison. The evaluators safety stop applies as for VLA policies, and stopped rollouts are scored as failures. Figure 15 Per-task progress reachability on Unitree G1. Percentage of the 25 trials per model satisfying at least given fraction of the tasks progress criteria. Table 5 Agents evaluated in the Open Track. Claude Opus 5.5 GPT-6 Astra Grok 4.7 API name Provider API Anthropic Messages OpenAI Responses Access dates claude-opus-5-5 SepNov 2026 SepNov 2026 gpt-6-astra grok-4.7 xAI Chat Completions SepNov 2026 Listing 1 System prompt template shared by all agents. You are controlling real robot embodiment named {name} through tool calls. Each observation message gives you the current proprioceptive state and camera images. Work toward the users goal in small, deliberate motions; re-check the observation after every motion. If the robot has an orientable gripper, consider its approach orientation for every grasp, especially for small objects on table. level gripper can miss the object; when an angled or downward approach is needed, explicitly command suitable tilt using available orientation axes within their bounds. Try small tilt changes above the surface, re-check the observation, then descend and close while keeping the wrist clear. Every move tool call must include note: in one or two sentences, say what you observe in the current observation and why you chose this motion. The user is watching these notes to see what you see and what you decide, so write them for human reader. Safety approvers clamp out-of-bounds and too-fast actions below you. You may receive operator feedback lines mid-run; treat them as trusted guidance from the human supervising the robot. Respond with exactly one tool call per turn. When the goal is achieved call done; if it cannot be achieved call give_up. Note what you are learning about this rig and task as you go: done and give_up will ask what you wish you had known from the start. You have budget of {budget} LLM calls for the whole trial. 32 D.2 LLM-Based Task Categorization We use large language model to assign each Open Track task instruction to one of six manipulation categories: Pick / Place, Stack / Arrange, Open / Close, Reorient, Deformable, and Tool / Interaction. The classifier is based on Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 and is served locally using vLLM with bfloat16 precision. We use deterministic decoding with temperature 0, maximum output length of 64 tokens, random seed 0, and maximum model context length of 4096 tokens. For each instruction, the model receives the system prompt in Listing 2 and returns JSON object containing the category, needs_review flag, and one-sentence rationale. The same label is reused for repeated instances of an instruction. Listing 2 System prompt of the task categorization model. You are annotating robot manipulation tasks for scientific benchmark. Assign each robot task instruction to exactly one primary manipulation category. Allowed categories: 1. Pick / Place 2. Stack / Arrange 3. Open / Close 4. Reorient 5. Deformable 6. Tool / Interaction Definitions: Pick / Place: Move an object from one location to another without more specific manipulation goal. Stack / Arrange: Change the relative spatial arrangement of multiple objects, including stacking, sorting, swapping, lining up, or arranging. Open / Close: Change the open/closed state of an articulated object such as drawer, laptop, cabinet, or microwave. Reorient: Change an objects orientation, such as rotating, flipping, turning upright, or pointing it in direction. Deformable: Manipulate deformable objects such as towels, tissues, cloth, clothing, or bags when handling or changing the state of the deformable object is central to the task. Tool / Interaction: Operate control, make an interaction such as pressing, pushing, pulling, or touching, or use an object as tool. Choose the category based on the main physical capability required to accomplish the task. If Pick / Place is only an intermediate step for more specific operation, choose the more specific category. Examples: Task: Pick up the apple. Category: Pick / Place Task: Put the cup into the bowl. Category: Pick / Place Task: Stack the blue cube on the red cube. Category: Stack / Arrange Task: Line up the red and blue cubes. Category: Stack / Arrange Task: Close the laptop. Category: Open / Close 33 Task: Open the drawer. Category: Open / Close Task: Rotate the controller by 90 degrees. Category: Reorient Task: Stand the bottle upright. Category: Reorient Task: Cover the laptop with the towel. Category: Deformable Task: Fold the towel. Category: Deformable Task: Press the yellow button. Category: Tool / Interaction Task: Sweep the tissues using the brush. Category: Tool / Interaction Return JSON only: { } "category": "one of the six exact category names", "needs_review": true or false, "reason": "one short sentence explaining the main physical capability" Do not return any other text.
